A B S T R A C T
Natural-hazard-triggered technological accidents (Natechs) pose compound risks to the process industries, yet
large historical databases remain under-utilized due to unstructured narratives and keyword-based screening. In
this work, we develop an automated, data-driven framework that fine-tunes generative large language models
(LLMs) to jointly (i) classify Natech status and the primary hazard, (ii) extract affected unit–issue pairs, and (iii)
generate brief, evidence-style justifications from incident text. Using the Texas Commission on Environmental
Quality (TCEQ) air emission event database (2004–2024) as a region-specific testbed, we construct a supervised
fine-tuning corpus via a schema-constrained template and evaluate the fine-tuned LLMs against LSTM and BERT
baselines. The best fine-tuned model leads on every metrics, with an overall accuracy of 0.958 and macro-F1 of
0.930, while a compact 3B variant remains competitive, demonstrating the superior performance and data ef
ficiency of pretrained transformers under constrained supervision. Applied at scale, the framework quantifies
climate-related patterns in Texas. By frequency, Natech incidents form ~6 % of statewide records, with counts
surging during extreme years (hurricanes in 2005, 2008 and 2017; winter freeze in 2021). By excessive emis
sions, Natech contributions ~10 % statewide and ~14 % in coastal Texas; along the coast, hurricanes dominate
and yield a disproportionately large share of Natech releases. The framework delivers single-pass, structured
analytics that reduce manual effort and improve reproducibility, providing decision-ready evidence for emer
gency preparedness and mitigation. Looking ahead, coupling the model with retrieval-grounded weather data
and human-in-the-loop audits could enable a production-grade Natech analytics agent for continuous monitoring
and planning.

Pollution, 2025), and European databases such as FACTS, eNATECH,

structured labels were present; otherwise, information had to be inferred
manually, limiting scalability and reproducibility. This workflow has

example, generic terms like “rain”, “wind”, or “cold” may be inter
changeable in context or may not indicate a Natech at all (Sengul et al.,
2012; Yang et al., 2025). Furthermore, manual verification coupled with
keyword search is time-consuming, if not infeasible, for large databases,
especially those lacking meaningful labels.

learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks

(CNNs) (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), often paired with word-embedding

incident-narrative classification. However, applications of AI/NLP to
Natech remain limited. The semi-intelligent Natech identification

deep-learning framework (LSTM/CNN) for Natech text classification on
the NRC database, achieving large-scale automated extraction but still
relying on keyword/word-index features and manual checks, which
constrains scaling to larger corpora. Moreover, effective Natech

This study proposes an automated, data-driven Natech analysi
framework based on fine-tuned LLMs. We cast information retrieval as a
constrained, multi-output generation task: (i) Natech flag and primary
hazard category, (ii) unit–issue pairs (e.g., “flare: over-pressure”), and

Environmental Quality (TCEQ) air emission event database (Texas
Commission on Enviromental Quality, 2025), covering two decades in
one of the U.S. regions most exposed to extreme weather, as a testbed to
build a region-specific model for large-scale historical analysis. The
pipeline comprises: (1) programmatic data curation and conversion of
narratives into a fine-tuning corpus with a fixed output schema; (2)
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of pretrained LLMs; (3) comparative eval
uation against BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and LSTM baselines; and (4)
model application and data analytics on Natech trends in Texas with
special focus on the Gulf Coast region. This paper (i) introduces a uni
fied, fine-tuned-LLM framework that performs Natech classification and
structured generation from incident narratives (ii) provides a
two-decade, region-specific analysis of climate-related releases for Texas
and coastal Texas using the TCEQ database (iii) demonstrates that
fine-tuned LLMs are a novel and promising tool for Natech database
analysis, enabling decision-ready evidence for preparedness and miti
gation planning.

We used the TCEQ database spanning 2004–2024. A template
example of the data structure is shown in Appendix Figure S1. Under 30
Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §101.1, an emission event involves
unauthorized emissions associated with upsets or unplanned mainte
nance/startup/shutdown activities: the database therefore directly tar-
gets hazmat release incidents. We focus on Texas, with particular

the high concentration of petrochemical assets and recurrent severe-
weather exposures, notably hurricanes and winter storms. Because
Natech occurrence is not geographically uniform, conclusions from
global or nationwide aggregates may underperform for regional risk
assessment; using local records provides a tighter empirical basis for
region-specific model development.

1) Deduplication. We merged records likely describing the same event
using a composite key of owner/operator, regulated entity, and
incident start datetime (and, when available, physical location). This
consolidation captures cases where a single hazard triggered releases
from multiple emission points and avoids inflating event counts or
leaking near-duplicate narratives across train/test splits. The dataset
size decreased from 93,958 to 82,089 records.
2) Pre-screening. To reduce computational cost while minimizing false
negatives, we applied a conservative keyword filter that included
both hazard-specific terms and generic, weather-adjacent terms that
are not necessarily climate-related (e.g., “cold”, “temperature”). This
step was intentionally recall-oriented, accepting more false positives
to ensure coverage of potential Natechs. This yielded 10,927 candi
dates for downstream analysis. A full list of keywords is shown in
Appendix Table S12.

Using synthetic data can significantly accelerate the data preparation
process. In typical industrial NLP settings, labeled Natech data are
scarce, but high-capacity teachers can already produce low-
hallucination, schema-conformant outputs when tightly prompted.
Distilling these references into a lighter model reduces compute and
memory requirements while preserving task competence, and it enables
more flexible human-in-the-loop refinement. From a deployment
standpoint, a fine-tuned open-source student model can approach
teacher-level accuracy while running on modest edge hardware,
yielding lower per-document cost and avoiding transmission of poten
tially confidential data to third-party services. By contrast, invoking a
large proprietary model at inference time typically entails higher cost,
external-API latency, and additional data-governance risk. Thus, once
task-adequate performance is established, smaller fine-tuned models
provide a more scalable, private, and controllable path to deployment
(Hinton et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).
2.3. Training/test set split
The corpus comprised 3000 incidents paired with teacher-generated
outputs (o3-mini). We adopted an 80/20 split (2400 training / 600 test).
Samples were drawn via stratified sampling so that the label distribu
tions in both subsets approximated that of the full corpus. Two classes,
strong wind and tornado, were extremely low resource. To avoid intro
ducing label/prior shift relative to the deployment distribution, we
preserved the natural class skew in both training and test sets rather than
oversampling. In previous studies, large pretrained models have
demonstrated data efficiency and can learn from few-shot examples
(Brown et al., 2020), there the current split was considered reasonable.
To evaluate the impact of class imbalance on minority-class perfor
mance, we reported macro-averaged metrics and per-class scores in
Section 3. The training/test set label distributions are shown in Fig. 2.

and add task-specific heads or embeddings at the input/output (head-

2.4. SFT via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
Training LLMs from scratch is infeasible for most engineering
research because it demands billions of tokens and weeks of multi-GPU
computation. Instead, a practical alternative is to fine-tune a pre-trained
base model that already encodes general linguistic and reasoning ca

and add task-specific heads or embeddings at the input/output (head-

variant is parameter-efficient but often suffers from representation
mismatch: the tiny head tends to over-fit the small domain corpus while
the frozen backbone cannot adapt, leading to sub-optimal use of the
pretrained knowledge (Houlsby et al., 2019). The second approach often
yields the best task performance but also incurs catastrophic forgetting,
i.e., erosion of the model’s general abilities when gradients overwrite
old knowledge (Chen et al., 2020; Li and Hoiem, 2017), besides, it is
much more memory- and storage-intensive.

representations that learn effectively from limited task data (Brown

modest improvement over BERT, with margins of around 2 %, con

4. Conclusion
We developed a fine-tuned LLM framework that turns chemica
emission narratives into structured Natech analytics at scale. Among all
models, the fine-tuned LLaMA-3.1–8B-Instruct delivers the best overall
classification performance, surpassing the BERT and LSTM baselines on
accuracy and macro metrics; the compact 3B variant also reached strong
macro-F1, underscoring the data efficiency of pretrained transformers
under limited, unbalanced supervision. Beyond classification, the sys
tem jointly performs information extraction (process units: issue pairs)
and short justifications, yielding a single-pass, auditable output that
reduces manual curation time and improves versatility.
Applying the framework to two decades of TCEQ events shows that
climate-related (Natech) releases are modest on average at the state
level (~10 % statewide; ~14 % in coastal Texas) yet episodic and surge-
prone, with sharp peaks during catastrophic hurricanes (2005, 2008,
2017) and severe freeze (2021). The risk is geographically differenti
ated: the Gulf Coast of Texas is hurricane-centric, where hurricane-
triggered events contribute a disproportionately large share of emis
sion mass, while the statewide pattern is multi-hazard, with freezing
cold and lightning remaining substantial components of the emission.
Taken together, these findings demonstrate that fine-tuned LLMs can
elevate Natech research from manual, keyword-driven review to auto
mated, explainable, and reproducible analytics that support seasonal
preparedness and long-term mitigation planning. The approach provides
a practical foundation for next-generation systems that couple LLM
reasoning with retrieval grounding and human-in-the-loop oversight,
enabling continuous improvement as new data and events accumulate.

Applying the framework to two decades of TCEQ events shows that
climate-related (Natech) releases are modest on average at the state
level (~10 % statewide; ~14 % in coastal Texas) yet episodic and surge-
prone, with sharp peaks during catastrophic hurricanes (2005, 2008,
2017) and severe freeze (2021). The risk is geographically differenti
ated: the Gulf Coast of Texas is hurricane-centric, where hurricane-
triggered events contribute a disproportionately large share of emis
sion mass, while the statewide pattern is multi-hazard, with freezing
cold and lightning remaining substantial components of the emission.
Taken together, these findings demonstrate that fine-tuned LLMs can
elevate Natech research from manual, keyword-driven review to auto
mated, explainable, and reproducible analytics that support seasonal
preparedness and long-term mitigation planning. The approach provides
a practical foundation for next-generation systems that couple LLM
reasoning with retrieval grounding and human-in-the-loop oversight,
enabling continuous improvement as new data and events accumulate.
